title: Which of these numbers are prime?
description: Six number cards are sorted by counting the factors of each one. A prime has exactly two factors, a composite has more than two, and one has a single factor. Keeko's doubt, that one is prime, is tested against the two-factor rule.
teaching_notes: One idea: count the factors, and exactly two means prime. Watch for students who call one prime because it has no factor but itself.

source: Which of 1, 2, 9, 13, 21 and 29 are prime? Give the factors
video_script.why: The child can list factors but has not yet used the count of factors to sort numbers into prime and composite.
video_script.substitution: Count the factors of each number: exactly two means prime, more than two means composite, and one factor means neither.
video_script.anchor: Six number cards in a row, marked one, two, nine, thirteen, twenty one and twenty nine.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one is prime because its only factor is itself. But a prime needs exactly two different factors, and one has only a single factor.
video_script.payoff_line: Two, thirteen and twenty nine are prime.

final_answer.value: 2, 13 and 29 are prime; 9 and 21 are composite; 1 is neither
final_answer.spoken: two, thirteen and twenty nine are prime, nine and twenty one are composite, and one is neither

maths_rules: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and the number itself. A composite number has more than two factors.
1 has only one factor, itself, so it is neither prime nor composite.
2: factors 1, 2, so prime. 13: factors 1, 13, so prime. 29: factors 1, 29, so prime.
9: factors 1, 3, 9, so composite. 21: factors 1, 3, 7, 21, so composite.
Slip: calling 1 prime fails because 1 has a single factor, not two.
video_script.design: One idea: count the factors, and exactly two means prime. Assumes the child can list factors. Wrong idea: one is prime. The six cards stay on the board all video.
